function.name: cmd_controller_execute
function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

unit.description: Specifies the unit of measure for the command if applicable. This is not utilized by os.system() directly but can be used for logging or analysis purposes.

message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact bandwidth you’re getting right now. But you can quickly find out yourself with a few different options: | Method | How to run it | What you’ll see | |--------|---------------|-----------------| | **Web‑based speed test** | Open a browser and go to (or any other speed‑test site). Click “Go” and wait for the download/upload results. | Download speed, upload speed, ping. | | **Command‑line (Windows)** | 1. Open PowerShell.
2. Run: `powershell -Command "Measure-Command { (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin', 'test.bin') }"`
3. Delete the test file afterward (`Remove-Item test.bin`). | The command prints the elapsed time; you can calculate speed = 100 MB / elapsed seconds. | | **Command‑line (Windows, if you have `speedtest-cli`)** | 1. Install it via pip: `pip install speedtest-cli` (you’ll need Python).
2. Run: `speedtest-cli --simple` | A concise output of ping, download, and upload speeds. | | **Command‑line (Linux/macOS)** | `curl -o /dev/null -w "%{speed_download}\n" https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin` | Prints the download speed in bytes/sec. | ### Quick PowerShell example If you just want a quick test without installing anything extra, try this: ```powershell # Measure download speed of a 100 MB test file $time = Measure-Command { (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile( 'https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin', 'C:\Temp\test.bin' ) } # Clean up Remove-Item 'C:\Temp\test.bin' # Convert elapsed time to seconds and compute speed $seconds = $time.TotalSeconds $bytes = 100 * 1024 * 1024 # 100 MB in bytes $speedBps = $bytes / $seconds $speedMbps = $speedBps / 1_000_000 "Download speed ≈ $([math]::Round($speedMbps,2)) Mbps" ``` Run that in PowerShell, and you’ll get an approximate download speed in Mbps. (Upload speed will need a separate test.) --- **Tip:** If you’re doing this regularly, consider installing `speedtest-cli` (Python) or the official Speedtest app from Ookla; they give you a full report (download, upload, ping, ISP info, etc.) with a single command.
